description.narrative:
The objective of this support is Building Inclusive and Multi-dimensional Approaches and Capacities for Effective Conflict Prevention in Africa.
The intervention covers 3 result areas: 1) Enhanced Institutional Responses of the AU and RECS to Prevent Complex Conflicts 2) Strengthened Capacities of National and Local Infrastructures for Effective Conflict Prevention 3) Enhanced Evidence Based Analysis to Inform Policy Support and Knowledge Production for Conflict Prevention
Key constituencies to the programme include local, national, and regional structures, such as the AU, RECs/RMs (IGAD, SADC, ECCAS), and other organisations such as the United Cities and Local Governments; Youth focused and youth-led organisations, Women focused, and women led organisations and Networks (FemWise-Africa and GIMAC); Community leaders; and Faith-based and traditional leaders.

sector.narrative: Civilian peace-building, conflict prevention and resolution

title.narrative: African Centre for the Constructive Resolution of Dispute (ACCORD)

description.narrative:
Key deliverables according to ACCORD has been the continued work with FemwiseSouth Sudan local chapter that resulted in the launch of the network. In addition, ACCORD has continued the consultations with AU mediation unit regarding the revision of the AU Mediation Handbook which is an important institutional tool for AU:s work on mediation.
On a regional level ACCORD has engaged with SADC in its work to develop a strategy for Youth Peace and Security. ACCORD has supported the review of the strategy to pave the way for its validation and eventuell adoption in 2025. On a South African level, ACCORD has worked with local NGO:s with the Women Peace and Security Agenda. ACCORD has contributed to the establishment of a National Action Plan (NAP) for UNSCR 1325. In 2024, ACCORD has continued this work to establish local awareness, knowledge and capacity development with regards to the NAP.
ACCORD has deepened its engagement with the Council of Swaziland Churches to strengthen the role of faith based leaders in conflict prevention. The aim of this cooperation is to establish Local Peace Committees with the aim of contributing to a local infrastructure for conflict prevention in a politically volatile environment.
These are some examples of how ACCORD has worked with conflict prevention in various processes and levels (regional, national and local) and with various actors (AU, faith based organisations and local NGO:s).
Recalling that the overall objective of the programme is to build inclusive and multidimensional approaches and capacities for effective conflict prevention in Africa, Sida assesses that the program will achieve its objectives with regards to local structures and with enhancing the role of women in peace processes in particular.
With regards to the institutional frameworks of AU and regional organisations such as IGAD and SADC, Sida assesses that ACCORD has had less institutional clout. As have been noted before, ACCORD does not have Memorandum of Understanding with neither AU nor the regional organisations which could provide a foundation for a more permanent institutional collaboration. The absence of this means that the role of ACCORD becomes more vague. For example, it has been noted that the role of the AU mission in South Sudan in supporting the Femwise network has over the years become less strong than what was originally envisioned. Sida assesses that the strongest institutional relationship has been built with Council of Swaziland Churches. This has probably to do with the local presence of ACCORD that facilitates collaboration.
ACCORD has intensified its work with Women, Peace and Security and works with four different women mediator's networks. This represents half of the processes that ACCORD is engaged in. The choice of this focus is unclear and it is not supported by a special emphasis on the outcome areas
Result based management:
With regards to result based management, it is noted that ACCORD has been responsive with regards to Sida's feedback in encourage ACCORD to elaborate more on the kind of processes and the nature of engagement. ACCORD has provided for the reporting of 2024 the inclusion of a second annex on processes and institutional relationships provided clarity on processes and institutional relationships. Sida could gather from this reporting that the depth of institutional relationships varies, it tends to be weaker with AU and the regional organisations and stronger with the national and local organisations.
ACCORD has demonstrated an ability to carry through and work on the goals it originally set up to do. The work on South Sudan FemWise has been continuous, as well as the collaboration with the faith based community in South Africa. Processes that relate to peacebuilding and conflict prevention take time. They are political processes, involve many counterparts and are time consuming. ACCORD has demonstrated an organisational perserverence in particular working with the WPS agenda as well as the faith based organisations. This has been positive. However, it could also have been more strategic in its strategy implementation, being more focused in its choice of partners, ensuring MoU:s with AU and the RECs.
A general observation is that the formulation of the program goals is expressed in a high level manner and do not necessarily resonate with the activities that shall contribute to the goal. For example, the narrative reporting does not provide information how the launch and training (two virtual meetings and one training session) of the FemWise local chapter of SouthSudan have enhanced the institutional response of the AU and RECs which is the goal that this activity is attributed to.
In conclusion, for the year of 2024, Sida assesses that: ACCORD has been able to sustain and carry on the implementation of previously decided decisions. The number of processes that focus on WPS accounts for half of the processes that ACCORD works with. The choice of this focus is unclear since the outcome areas do not give instructions to focus more on WPS than other thematic areas. The depth of institutional collaboration is generally quite restricted to participation and providing workshops and other services. ACCORD seem to have a more operative role with one institution, Council of Swaziland Churches. In some areas, for example the work with Femwise in South Sudan, the role of the AU has become vaguer over time.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
